source: Schubert, Jagadish, Binz, Schulz (2024) In-context learning agents are asymmetric belief updaters
finding: A prompted Claude v1.3 learned a two-option slot machine task by in-context learning. A Rescorla-Wagner model with separate learning rates for positive and negative prediction errors fitted best. The model learned much more from positive errors, like humans but with a bigger gap.
numbers: Partial feedback, 50 simulated runs, temperature 0. Regret fell from 0.09 to 0.05 (t(199)=3.1, p=.002). Asymmetric RW model posterior probability 0.93. alpha+ = 0.87, alpha- = 0.10 (t(49)=20.1, p<.0001). Human data (Lefebvre 2017) show the same sign but a smaller gap.
quote: In-context learning agents are asymmetric belief updaters.
limits: One model (Claude v1.3), one temperature, one paradigm family. Learning rates are fitted descriptions of behaviour, not proof of an internal RPE.
agent_relevance: An LLM in a loop treats good news as more informative than bad news. Feedback to a scaffold should be framed so failures are not underweighted.

source: Schubert, Jagadish, Binz, Schulz (2024) In-context learning agents are asymmetric belief updaters (full-feedback block)
finding: When the foregone outcome of the unchosen option was shown, the optimism bias held for the chosen option but reversed for the unchosen option. This pattern is called confirmation bias in humans.
numbers: 24 runs, 16 blocks of 40 trials. Final regret 0.07 (partial) vs 0.02 (full), t(191)=2.9, p=.004. Chosen option optimism t(23)=5.9, p<.0001. Unchosen option pessimism t(23)=5.7, p<.0001. Merged confirmatory/disconfirmatory model posterior probability 0.92.
limits: Same single model and task family. Human numbers are reproduced from Chambon et al. 2020, not re-run.
agent_relevance: Counterfactual evidence is used, but weighted by whether it confirms the earlier choice. A critic step should be told to weigh disconfirming evidence equally.

source: Schubert, Jagadish, Binz, Schulz (2024) In-context learning agents are asymmetric belief updaters (agency manipulation)
finding: Asymmetry vanished when outcomes came from another agent (forced choices). Free-choice outcomes were still updated asymmetrically. A small meta-RL transformer trained from scratch showed the same asymmetry.
numbers: Mixed blocks: 40 free plus 40 forced trials, 24 runs. Regret 0.07 to 0.02 (t(143)=2.5, p=0.01). The LLM learned faster than humans in this condition. Forced-choice learning rates were symmetric.
limits: The reading (the model acts as if it owns its choices) is inferred. No ablation of prompt wording is given.
agent_relevance: Bias depends on ownership of the choice. Third-person evidence (other agents, logs) may be weighed more evenly than self-generated outcomes.

source: Hayes, Yax, Palminteri (2024) Relative value biases in large language models
finding: GPT-4 Turbo and Llama-2-70B chose between option pairs with repeated feedback. Both showed relative value bias (prefer options that were best locally, even with lower absolute payoff), like humans and animals. Asking the model to estimate expected outcomes before choosing removed the bias.
numbers: 30 runs per model. GPT-4 Turbo chose the locally optimal option about 99% of the time by trial 5 (t(29)=59, p<.001, d=10.77). Llama-2-70B about 82% (d=1.46). GPT-3.5-Turbo 71% (d=0.95). Llama-2-13B 58% (not above chance). Bias in GPT-4 Turbo only when the payoff gap was small (3 dollars). The expected-outcome prompt almost eliminated bias. Explicit comparison text increased it.
quote: Instructing the models to think about and estimate expected outcomes prior to making a choice all but eliminated relative value biases.
limits: Only the two best models analysed. Llama-2-70B bias was weak and noisy. Imitation of human text in training data cannot be ruled out.
agent_relevance: A simple prompt step (state expected values in absolute terms before choosing) removes a context-dependent bias. This maps to an agent step that restates absolute value before comparing options.

source: Hayes, Yax, Palminteri (2024/2025) Large language models are biased reinforcement learners (relative value encoding, multi-task)
finding: Across five bandit tasks and four chat models, a standard prompt gave a significant relative value bias in 2 of 5 tasks. A prompt with explicit outcome comparisons gave it in 4 of 5. Relative-encoding RL models fit best.
numbers: 1,200 runs (5 tasks x 4 LLMs x 2 prompts x 30). Relative-value choice rate .829 (comparisons) vs .698 (standard), F(1,1159)=440.88, p<.001, eta2=0.28. Relative-encoding weight .264 vs .131 (d=0.93). Learning rates confirmatory .483 vs disconfirmatory .166 (standard). Training accuracy .815 vs .746. Transfer accuracy .734 vs .771 (comparisons hurt transfer). GPT-4 was near ceiling and did not benefit. In gemma-7b hidden states, relative value was significant in 3% of units (standard) and 72% (comparisons).
limits: Chat/instruction-tuned models only. No human comparison numbers. The expected-outcome prompt was not retested in this paper.
agent_relevance: Prompts that invite comparison help in-context learning but hurt out-of-context transfer. Keep comparisons local and re-score absolute values at the end.

source: Demircan, Saanum, Jagadish, Binz, Schulz (2024) Sparse autoencoders reveal temporal difference learning in large language models
finding: Llama 3 70B solved a two-step RL task in context. Sparse autoencoder features in the residual stream tracked the TD error of a Q-learning agent. Switching those features off hurt behaviour. This is the closest LLM analogue of a dopamine RPE signal.
numbers: Best TD-error feature in block 34 had r=0.58 with the Q-learning TD error. In the graph task, latents with r>=0.75 were found from block 40 onward. Successor-representation task: max r=0.62 with the SR vs 0.49 with the transition matrix. TD error r=0.60 vs surprise signal r=0.18. Lesioning the strongest TD latent (block 64) cut next-state accuracy from 24.3% to 18.9%. Clamping a latent to -10 lowered Q-value and TD correlations.
quote: these representations emerge despite the model only being trained to predict the next token.
limits: Preprint, one model family. Correlation of a feature with a fitted TD error does not prove the model computes it that way. Features were selected for high correlation; the control used the lowest-correlation latents.
agent_relevance: In-context learning in LLMs likely uses an internal TD-like error. A prediction-error readout from activations could become a gate for what an agent stores or revises (open-weights models only).

source: Wang, Blaser, Daneshmand, Zhang (2025) Transformers can learn temporal difference methods for in-context reinforcement learning
finding: Proved that an L-layer linear transformer forward pass can implement batch TD(0) policy evaluation, and showed that training on policy-evaluation tasks makes the transformer learn this. Residual-gradient and multi-step variants also covered.
numbers: Theorem 1: forward pass equals TD(0) with a preconditioner. Theorem 2: Algorithm 1 training ends at the Theorem 1 solution for L=2, 3, 4 (and L=1 by Corollary).
limits: Authors state limits: policy evaluation only, no control. Linear attention and small synthetic Markov reward processes. ICLR 2025.
agent_relevance: Gives a mechanistic reason why a frozen model can learn values from a prompt with no weight updates, so RPE-style updating inside the context window is plausible.

source: Song, Moeini, Wang, Gong, Chandra, Zhang, Qi (2026) Reward is enough: LLMs are in-context reinforcement learners
finding: ICRL prompting: after each answer the model gets only a scalar reward. The next prompt holds all earlier answers with their rewards. Quality rises as context grows and beats Self-Refine and Reflexion, even when the reward comes from the same LLM.
numbers: Game of 24 (GPT-4.1): CoT-only 6%, Long-CoT 47%, Reflexion 44%, Best-of-N 49%, Self-Refine 47%, ICRL Preset 90%, ICRL Autonomous 84%. Creative writing length-controlled win rate vs Reflexion 59.48%, vs Long-CoT 78.36%, vs Self-Refine 86.32%, vs Best-of-N 93.81%. ScienceWorld: about 20% higher return than baselines after enough iterations.
limits: The Preset variant alternates explore and exploit instructions by hand. Game of 24 reward is the model's own 0-3 judgement. A growing context costs tokens. ICLR 2026.
agent_relevance: A direct scaffold: keep a log of attempts with numeric scores and ask for a better attempt. Cheap, no training. The scalar reward carries the error signal across trials.

source: Song et al. (2026) Reward is enough: mechanistic analysis of reward-aware attention heads
finding: In Qwen3-32B, many attention heads track the reward labels of earlier responses. Some attend more to high-reward responses, others to low-reward ones.
numbers: Of 2,048 heads in the last 32 layers, 597 (29.1%) were significant versus 102 (5%) expected by chance. 249 positive, 348 negative. 100 questions x 5 trials = 500 observations per head, reward labels randomised to 1 or 10.
limits: Correlational, one model, one task (creative writing). Multiple-comparison correction not stated in what I read.
agent_relevance: Supports learning from failures as well as successes through attention. Negative examples are not wasted.

source: Song et al. (2026) Reward is enough: ablations and model range
finding: ICRL beat Self-Refine and Reflexion across several open models on creative writing and AIME. Exploration-only and recent-3-episode variants were weaker.
numbers: Rows read: creative-writing length-controlled win rate Self-Refine 46.33, 45.83, 44.41 vs Reflexion 42.73, 40.87, 40.72. AIME solved Self-Refine 33.33/43.33/43.33, Reflexion 30.00/30.00/33.33. Best-of-N and Reflexion plateau quickly.
limits: I extracted only the baseline rows of this table, not the ICRL rows. Compute budgets differ between methods.
agent_relevance: Exploration instructions matter. A score history without an instruction to vary the attempt plateaus.

source: Binz, Schulz (2023) Using cognitive psychology to understand GPT-3
finding: GPT-3 (davinci, temperature 0) did well on a bandit task but showed no directed exploration. It beat humans on average regret in the horizon task.
numbers: Horizon task: GPT-3 mean regret 2.72 (SD 5.98) vs humans 3.24 (SD 10.26). Decisions from descriptions: below human level (t(29134)=-11.50, p<.001) over 13,000 problems. Random exploration present, but no horizon interaction (no strategic noise) and no information-seeking effect (no directed exploration). Only the largest GPT-3 model solved the bandit.
quote: shows no signatures of directed exploration
limits: Old model (2022), single prompt format. Later models behave differently (see Zhang 2025, Centaur).
agent_relevance: Base models of 2022 exploited well but did not seek information on purpose. Exploration needs scaffolding.

source: Binz, Schulz (2023) Using cognitive psychology to understand GPT-3 (two-step task)
finding: On the Daw two-step task GPT-3 showed signatures of model-based reasoning, not the purely model-free RPE-driven strategy that dopamine models describe.
numbers: Qualitative statement in the paper (discussion section). I did not extract the effect size.
limits: A model-based signature in a text task can come from reading the task description. Debates over how clean the human model-free/model-based split is also apply.
agent_relevance: Language models plan from the prompt. Pure model-free habit learning is not their default.

source: Krishnamurthy, Harris, Foster, Zhang, Slivkins (2024) Can large language models explore in-context?
finding: GPT-3.5, GPT-4 and Llama2 did not explore robustly in bandits. Only one configuration worked: GPT-4 with chain-of-thought, a hint to explore, and an externally summarised history.
numbers: GPT-4 basic prompt: suffix failure in more than 60% of replicates (T=500, N=20), like Greedy. GPT-4 with suggestive framing, summary and CoT: unimodal best-arm plays, few suffix failures (T=200, N=40). 48 configurations for GPT-3.5 and Llama2, 72 for GPT-4. About 200K queries for GPT-3.5, 50K for GPT-4.
quote: only one configuration resulted in satisfactory exploratory behavior
limits: Small bandit instances. The working recipe needs an external summary step, which may be hard in complex tasks.
agent_relevance: If an agent must explore, give it computed summary statistics (counts, means) instead of raw logs, and tell it to explore.

source: Nie et al. (2024/2025) EVOLvE: evaluating and optimizing LLMs for in-context exploration (BanditBench)
finding: Gemma and Gemini models stay below UCB on bandits. Algorithm-guided support (UCB-style statistics in the prompt) and fine-tuning on UCB trajectories helped most.
numbers: Win rate %: Raw History Flash 27.7, Pro 45.5. Summarized History Flash 34.8, Pro 60.0. Algorithm-Guided Flash 32.2, Pro 59.6. UCB 90.6 (Flash set) to 96.4 (Pro set). Contextual bandit, Pro: 7.1 raw to 64.3 with algorithm guidance (K=10). Fraction of pulls on best arm after 1000 steps: UCB 65.0%, Flash 10.7 to 16.8%. Gemma 2B and 9B stayed linear in regret.
limits: I read only the first 100K characters. Some tables and text disagree. Few-shot hurt Pro but helped Flash. UCB is the only oracle.
agent_relevance: Handing the model a classical value statistic closes much of the gap. Give the agent computed value tables instead of asking it to infer them from text.

source: Zhang, Wang, Chen, Mansur, Sarhangian (2025) Comparing exploration-exploitation strategies of LLMs and humans on standard multi-armed bandit tasks
finding: Reasoning-enhanced models moved toward the human mix of random and directed exploration in simple stationary bandits. In harder non-stationary tasks they still did not match humans.
numbers: 2-armed task: basic LLMs showed random exploration but little directed exploration or perseveration. Reasoning raised directed exploration, with ChatGPT and DeepSeek reasoning versions above human level. 4-armed task: all LLM directed-exploration coefficients stayed negative and random exploration was higher than humans. Models: GPT-4o-mini, Gemini-1.5-pro, DeepSeek-V3 and reasoning counterparts.
limits: Numeric tables are in the appendix, which I did not read. Model naming in the paper is inconsistent.
agent_relevance: Reasoning mode produces more human-like uncertainty-driven exploration. Turn reasoning on when exploration matters.

source: Coda-Forno, Binz, Wang, Schulz (2024) CogBench: a large language model walks into a psychology lab
finding: A benchmark of seven psychology tasks (including horizon, restless bandit, instrumental learning, two-step task) scored 35 LLMs. Almost all showed a strong optimism bias and high learning rates, and weighted priors over observations.
numbers: 35 LLMs. Parameter count raised model-basedness (beta=0.481, z=4.2, p<.001). Chain-of-thought raised probabilistic reasoning by 9.01% and model-basedness by 64.59%. Take-a-step-back raised reasoning 3.10% and model-basedness 118.59%. RLHF models were closer to human behaviour.
limits: Temperature 0, one prompt per task. Percent changes are relative to base models on a model-basedness score.
agent_relevance: Prompt scaffolds (chain-of-thought, step-back) shift an LLM toward planning from a world model and away from reactive updating.

source: Binz et al. (2025) A foundation model to predict and capture human cognition (Centaur)
finding: Llama 3.1 70B fine-tuned on Psych-101 (160 experiments, 60,092 participants, 10,681,650 choices) predicts human choices in bandit and two-step tasks better than most cognitive RL models. Its internals predicted accumbens activity, the region with an RPE effect in the original two-step study, better than Llama or a cognitive model.
numbers: Average negative log-likelihood: Centaur 0.44, Llama 0.58, domain cognitive models 0.56 (better in all but one experiment). Held-out table rows (columns read as Centaur, Llama, cognitive model): horizon task 0.4032, 0.5237, 0.3595 (cognitive model better); two-step 0.4998, 0.6075, 0.6043. New three-armed bandit: Centaur 0.42, Llama 0.62, cognitive model 0.98. Open-loop horizon simulation: human-like directed exploration.
limits: Column order inferred, not verified. Critics question generalisation (arXiv 2604.27927, not opened). Needs a 70B model and fine-tuning.
agent_relevance: Fine-tuning on trial-by-trial human choices gives a simulator of how people learn from reward. It predicts people. It is not a thinking scaffold.

source: Song and Xin (2026) D-MEM: dopamine-gated agentic memory via reward prediction error routing
finding: An LLM-agent memory system borrows the dopamine RPE idea. Each new input gets a surprise-times-utility score. Low scores skip memory work, high scores trigger deep knowledge-graph updates. This is a direct use of RPE gating inside an agent loop.
numbers: LoCoMo-Noise (75% noise), GPT-4o-mini: overall F1 0.369 vs A-MEM 0.336. Tokens 319K vs 1,648K (-80%). Adversarial 0.412 vs 0.388. Standard LoCoMo: overall F1 37.4%, multi-hop 42.7% vs 27.0%, but single-hop 21.6% vs A-MEM 44.7%. Thresholds 0.3 and 0.7.
limits: The signal is not a reward error. Surprise is embedding distance to memory and utility is an LLM score. Preprint, one backbone, own benchmark, thresholds tuned on it. The skip rule loses short factual items. Some numbers in text and table disagree.
agent_relevance: A cheap gate for our agent's memory writes: store or revise only on surprising and useful items. Watch the single-hop loss.

source: Shinn et al. (2023) Reflexion: language agents with verbal reinforcement learning
finding: Reflexion turns scalar or binary feedback into a written reflection stored in memory and used on the next trial. This is an agent-loop analogue of learning from an error signal without weight updates.
numbers: Not read this session. In Song et al. 2026 it scored 44% on Game of 24 vs ICRL 90%.
limits: The number is from the ICRL paper's table, not from Reflexion itself.
agent_relevance: Verbal error feedback works but plateaued faster than scalar-reward histories in the Song et al. comparison.

source: Schultz, Dayan, Montague (1997) A neural substrate of prediction and reward
finding: Classic TD account of dopamine neuron firing. Demircan et al. cite the neuroscience line (TD error linked to dopamine) as motivation for looking for TD errors in LLMs.
numbers: Not read this session. No numbers recorded.
limits: Background only. Listed to link the LLM TD-latent work to the neural original.
agent_relevance: Defines the signal the LLM studies above look for in activations.

source: Wilson, Geana, White, Ludvig, Cohen (2014) Humans use directed and random exploration to solve the explore-exploit dilemma
finding: The horizon task separates directed exploration (information bonus) from random exploration (decision noise). It is the test used for LLMs in Binz and Schulz 2023, CogBench and Centaur.
numbers: Not read this session.
limits: Referenced through the LLM papers only. DOI not verified.
agent_relevance: Gives the yardstick for whether an agent explores on purpose.

source: Palminteri and Lebreton (2022) The computational roots of positivity and confirmation biases in reinforcement learning
finding: Source of the confirmatory vs disconfirmatory learning-rate account used by Schubert et al. and Hayes et al. to describe LLM updating.
numbers: Not read this session.
limits: Cited in the LLM papers. DOI not verified.
agent_relevance: Names the bias the agent should guard against: updating more when evidence confirms the earlier choice.

source: Cross-check: Krishnamurthy 2024 vs Zhang 2025 on bandit exploration
finding: Two studies a year apart agree that plain prompting fails at directed exploration. Either CoT plus a summary (2024) or reasoning models (2025) brings it back.
numbers: 2024: 1 of 48 to 72 configurations succeeded. 2025: reasoning versions of GPT, Gemini and DeepSeek increased directed exploration relative to base models.
limits: Different task sets and models, no common metric. The cross-check is mine, not either paper's claim.
agent_relevance: Rule of thumb for the scaffold: exploration needs reasoning on and computed history statistics.

source: Other 2026 agent-memory work gated by surprise or prediction error (ReSuME, PreCoMem, belief-based memory 2606.22030)
finding: Search results list several 2026 papers that gate memory writes by a surprise or prediction-error signal (SAE reconstruction error in ReSuME, effective surprisal in PreCoMem, contradiction-driven belief updating in 2606.22030).
numbers: Not opened. No numbers recorded.
limits: Only search snippets seen. Ids and venues unverified.
agent_relevance: The RPE-gated memory idea is spreading. Check before relying on any of them.

source: Le et al. (2023) Beyond surprise: improving exploration through surprise novelty
finding: RL intrinsic-motivation work using prediction error as reward. An associative memory stops repeated predictable errors from giving reward (the noisy-TV problem).
numbers: Not opened.
limits: RL, not LLM. Snippet only.
agent_relevance: A raw surprise gate can be fooled by unpredictable but useless noise. D-MEM adds a utility gate for this reason.
